name: Flat Bench Press
description: The classic horizontal pressing movement. Builds overall upper-body pushing strength with a barbell and bench. A foundational compound lift that also challenges the shoulders and triceps.
startingPosition: Lie on a flat bench with your feet planted firmly on the floor. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width and unrack it above your chest with straight arms.
steps: Set the safety pins or ask for a spot before you unrack any working weight.
Lower the bar slowly to your mid-chest with elbows at about 45° from your body.
Touch the chest lightly — do not bounce the bar.
Press the bar back up in a straight line until your arms are extended.
Keep your shoulder blades squeezed together and feet grounded for every rep.
breathing: Inhale as you lower the bar, exhale forcefully as you press it up.

beginner.note: Start with the empty bar or light dumbbells until the movement feels natural. Always use a spotter.

intermediate.note: Progress the load gradually (2.5 kg per side per week is plenty).

advanced.note: Consider periodisation and always keep a spotter for heavy sets.

commonMistakes: Bouncing the bar off the chest
Lifting the hips off the bench
Not using a spotter on heavy sets
safetyTips: Learn proper technique from a qualified trainer before performing this exercise independently.
Always use safety pins or a spotter.
Never attempt a maximum-weight lift without supervision.
whenToStop: Sharp pain in the shoulder or chest
Loss of control of the bar
tip: A controlled 2-second lowering phase builds more strength than a fast drop — and is far safer.

name: Incline Bench Press
description: A bench press performed on a 30–45° incline to emphasise the upper chest and front shoulders. A staple for a balanced, strong chest.
startingPosition: Lie on an incline bench set to 30–45°. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width and unrack it above your upper chest.
steps: Set the bench angle to 30–45° — steeper angles shift work to the shoulders.
Lower the bar under control to just below your collarbone.
Pause for a moment without bouncing.
Press back up and slightly back until arms are extended.
Keep your back against the pad and feet flat on the floor throughout.
breathing: Inhale on the way down, exhale as you press up.

beginner.note: Use dumbbells or the Smith machine first if balancing the bar feels difficult.

intermediate.note: Alternate with flat pressing to develop the full chest.

advanced.note: Keep a spotter for working sets near failure.

safetyTips: Use a spotter or safety pins on heavy sets.
Stop if you feel pinching in the front of the shoulder.
tip: Keep the angle at 30–45°. Beyond that it becomes a shoulder press.

name: Chest Press Machine
description: A guided horizontal press on a fixed path. Ideal for learning the pressing pattern safely and for controlled, stable chest work.
startingPosition: Adjust the seat so the handles are level with your mid-chest. Sit with your back flat against the pad and grip the handles.
steps: Adjust the seat so the handles align with your mid-chest.
Select an appropriate resistance.
Position your back against the pad and plant your feet.
Grip the handles comfortably.
Press the handles forward with controlled movement until arms are extended.
Return slowly to the start without letting the weight stack touch down.
breathing: Exhale as you press forward, inhale as you return.

beginner.note: A great first machine — master control before moving to free weights.

intermediate.note: Use a slow 3-second return to increase time under tension.

advanced.note: Use as a finisher after free-weight pressing.

safetyTips: Use an appropriate resistance and stop if you experience sharp pain, dizziness, or unusual symptoms.
Never encourage unsafe maximum-weight lifting.
whenToStop: Inability to complete the return slowly
tip: Return the handles until you feel a gentle chest stretch — no further.

name: Pec Deck
description: A seated fly movement that isolates the chest through a hugging motion. Excellent for building chest definition with minimal shoulder stress.
startingPosition: Sit with your back flat, feet planted, and elbows placed against the pads at shoulder height, bent to about 90°.
steps: Adjust the seat so your elbows and shoulders are in line.
Keep a slight bend in the elbows for the entire set.
Squeeze the pads together until they almost touch.
Pause and squeeze the chest for one second.
Open the arms slowly until you feel a gentle stretch across the chest.
breathing: Exhale as the pads come together, inhale as they open.

beginner.note: Use a light resistance and focus on feeling the chest stretch and squeeze.

intermediate.note: Slow down the opening phase to about 3 seconds.

advanced.note: Use as a pre-exhaust or finisher exercise.

commonMistakes: Opening the arms too far past the chest line
Using momentum to swing the weight
safetyTips: Never let the arms travel behind the line of the body — the stretch comes from the chest, not the shoulder joint.
Keep the movement smooth.
whenToStop: Pain in the front of the shoulder
Clicking or catching in the shoulder joint
tip: Imagine hugging a barrel, not clapping — the elbows stay softly bent.

name: Cable Crossover
description: A standing cable fly with pulleys set high. Emphasises the inner chest and trains constant tension through the full range of motion.
startingPosition: Set the pulleys to shoulder height or slightly above. Hold a handle in each hand, step forward into a staggered stance and lean slightly forward.
steps: Set both pulleys at the same height.
Step forward so the cables are under light tension even at the start.
With a soft elbow bend, bring the handles together in front of your chest in an arc.
Squeeze the chest for one second at the meeting point.
Open the arms slowly, controlling the return, until you feel a stretch.
breathing: Exhale as the hands meet, inhale as they open.

beginner.note: Use light resistance and a slow, steady rhythm.

intermediate.note: Vary pulley height between sets for a fuller chest stimulus.

advanced.note: Try a 2-second squeeze at the top of each rep.

commonMistakes: Bending and straightening the elbows to "press" the weight
Using too much weight and swinging
safetyTips: Keep your core braced and spine neutral in the staggered stance.
Choose a resistance you can stop smoothly at any point.
tip: Fix the elbow angle once and move from the shoulder — the arm should never change shape during the rep.

name: Lat Pulldown
description: A vertical pulling movement that builds the lats — the wide muscles that create the V-shape of the back. A beginner-friendly route toward pull-ups.
startingPosition: Sit at the machine with your thighs secured under the pads. Grip the bar wider than shoulder width with palms facing forward, arms fully extended.
steps: Adjust the thigh pads so you stay seated during the pull.
Grip the bar just wider than shoulder width.
Lean back slightly, keep the chest up, and pull the bar to your upper chest.
Drive the elbows down and back, not just the hands.
Pause for a second, then let the bar rise under control until the arms are straight.
breathing: Exhale as you pull down, inhale as the bar rises.

beginner.note: Learn to feel the lats work; lighter is better than jerky.

intermediate.note: Try a pause at the chest on every rep.

advanced.note: Slow the negative to 3 seconds for extra back growth.

commonMistakes: Pulling the bar behind the neck
Swinging the torso to move the weight
safetyTips: Always pull to the front of the chest, never behind the neck.
Keep the movement controlled from start to finish.
whenToStop: Sharp pain in the shoulders or elbows
Feeling of the shoulder "popping" during the pull
tip: Think "elbows into your back pockets" — that cue turns the movement into a lat exercise.

name: Seated Cable Row
description: A horizontal pulling movement for mid-back thickness. The seated position keeps the spine supported, making it a safe rowing option for all levels.
startingPosition: Sit with feet braced on the platform, knees slightly bent, back straight. Hold the handle with arms extended, chest up.
steps: Sit tall with a neutral spine and soft knees.
Pull the handle toward your lower ribs.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the end of the pull.
Keep the elbows close to your sides.
Return slowly, letting the shoulders stretch forward without rounding the lower back.
breathing: Exhale as you pull, inhale as you return.

beginner.note: Keep the torso still — if it moves, reduce the weight.

intermediate.note: Pause for 1 second with the handle at the ribs.

advanced.note: Use different grips (narrow, wide) across sets.

commonMistakes: Rocking the torso back and forth
Rounding the lower back at the end of the return
Pulling to the neck instead of the ribs
safetyTips: Keep the lower back neutral throughout — brace as if someone might push you.
Never yank the first rep; begin the pull smoothly.
whenToStop: Inability to keep the torso still
tip: Imagine pulling your elbows back, not your hands — this keeps the biceps from taking over.

name: Assisted Pull-Up
description: The pull-up pattern with adjustable counterweight support. The best way to build the strength for full bodyweight pull-ups.
startingPosition: Kneel or stand on the assist platform, grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width, and let the counterweight support you with arms extended.
steps: Select an assist level that lets you complete every rep with good form.
Start from a full hang with the chest up.
Pull until your chin reaches bar height.
Lower yourself slowly until the arms are fully straight.
Reduce the assistance over the weeks as you get stronger.
breathing: Exhale as you pull up, inhale on the way down.

beginner.note: Choose generous assistance and prioritise a full range of motion.

intermediate.note: Lower the assistance each week until you can do unassisted reps.

advanced.note: Add a slow 3-second negative on the last rep of each set.

commonMistakes: Not reaching a full hang at the bottom
Pulling to the nose instead of the chest
safetyTips: Grip firmly and step off the platform carefully after the set.
Keep the core engaged so the body does not swing.
tip: Full range of motion beats half reps — lower all the way to a dead hang every time.

name: T-Bar Row
description: A supported bent-over row variation that allows heavy loading for mid-back thickness. The chest pad version keeps the lower back safe.
startingPosition: Load the bar, place your chest on the pad (or hinge at the hips for the free version), grip the handles with a neutral grip and let the weight hang.
steps: Keep your chest firmly on the pad for the entire set.
Start from a full stretch with the shoulder blades spread.
Row the weight up until the plates touch the chest pad.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together hard at the top.
Lower under control until the arms are straight.
breathing: Exhale as you row, inhale as you lower.

beginner.note: Master the chest-pad version before trying the free-standing hinge.

intermediate.note: Add a 1-second squeeze at the top of each rep.

advanced.note: Progress load conservatively; form quality is the goal.

commonMistakes: Letting the chest lift off the pad
Cutting the range of motion short
safetyTips: This is a heavier compound movement — learn proper technique from a qualified trainer before performing this exercise independently.
Keep the spine neutral; the pad should do the supporting.
whenToStop: Inability to keep the chest on the pad
tip: Think "pull with the elbows and squeeze at the top" — the squeeze is where the back grows.

name: Leg Press
description: A guided squat-pattern machine for lower-body strength. Supports the back while letting you train the legs hard.
startingPosition: Sit with your back and hips flat against the pad. Place your feet shoulder-width on the platform and release the safety handles.
steps: Adjust the seat so your knees stay at about 90° at the bottom.
Lower the platform until your knees approach your chest without the hips rolling up.
Keep your knees tracking in line with your toes.
Press through the whole foot back to the start without locking the knees hard.
Re-engage the safety handles before you get off.
breathing: Inhale as you lower, exhale as you press.

beginner.note: Learn the depth that keeps your hips on the pad.

intermediate.note: Vary foot placement: higher for glutes, lower for quads.

advanced.note: Use single-leg presses to address side-to-side differences.

commonMistakes: Locking the knees violently at the top
Letting the hips curl off the pad at the bottom
Placing the feet too low on the platform
safetyTips: Never fully lock and snap the knees.
Always confirm the safety handles are engaged before loading or exiting.
whenToStop: Knee pain that worsens during the press
Feeling of the hips lifting off the pad
tip: A controlled 3-second lowering phase turns the leg press into a much more effective builder.

name: Leg Extension
description: An isolation movement for the front of the thigh. Great for quad development, knee-friendly training, and finishing leg days.
startingPosition: Sit with the back against the pad, the knee joint aligned with the machine axis, and the shin pad resting just above your ankles.
steps: Adjust the seat so your knees line up with the pivot point of the machine.
Grip the handles for stability.
Extend your legs until they are straight, squeezing the quads.
Pause briefly at the top without locking out hard.
Lower slowly, controlling the weight all the way down.
breathing: Exhale as you extend, inhale as you lower.

beginner.note: Use light resistance and a full, smooth range of motion.

intermediate.note: Slow the lowering phase to 3 seconds.

advanced.note: Use as a pre-exhaust before squats or a finisher after.

commonMistakes: Kicking the weight up with momentum
Letting the hips lift off the seat
Only doing half range of motion
safetyTips: If you have a history of knee issues, consult a qualified professional before adding load.
Keep the movement smooth — no jerking.
tip: Point your toes up toward your knees during the lift for a stronger quad contraction.

name: Leg Curl
description: An isolation movement for the back of the thigh. Balances the legs by strengthening the hamstrings that squats and leg presses miss.
startingPosition: Lie face down (or sit, depending on the machine) with the knee joint aligned with the pivot and the pad resting above your heels.
steps: Align your knees with the machine pivot.
Grip the handles and press your hips down into the pad.
Curl the pad toward your glutes in a smooth arc.
Squeeze the hamstrings at the top.
Lower slowly until the knees are almost straight.
breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as you lower.

beginner.note: Keep the hips pressed down — do not let them rise.

intermediate.note: Add a 1-second squeeze at the top.

advanced.note: Try one leg at a time to fix imbalances.

commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the weight
safetyTips: Aim for the hamstrings to cramp-squeeze — not the lower back.
If you feel it in the calves or lower back, reduce the weight.
tip: Think of dragging the pad with your heels for a stronger hamstring contraction.

name: Squat Rack
description: The king of lower-body movements: the barbell back squat. Builds total-body strength, posture, and athletic power. Must be learned with proper coaching.
startingPosition: Set the bar at chest height, step under it with it resting on your upper back, grip it firmly, stand up, and walk two small steps back.
steps: Set the safety pins just below your bottom position.
Brace your core as if preparing to be pushed.
Sit down and back, keeping your chest proud and knees tracking over the toes.
Descend until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor.
Drive up through the mid-foot to stand.
Re-rack by walking the bar into the uprights — never while fatigued and never jumping it in.
breathing: Big inhale and brace before you descend, exhale as you pass the sticking point on the way up.

beginner.note: Learn the bodyweight and goblet squat first. Always squat inside a rack with pins.

intermediate.note: Film your sets from the side to check depth and bar path.

advanced.note: Programme deload weeks and never train heavy without a spotter or pins.

commonMistakes: Half-depth squats with too much weight
safetyTips: Learn proper technique from a qualified trainer before performing this exercise independently.
Always squat inside a rack with the safety pins set correctly.
Never attempt unsafe maximum-weight lifts.
whenToStop: Any feeling of losing balance with a loaded bar
tip: Push the floor apart with your feet — this keeps the knees out and the glutes engaged.

name: Smith Machine
description: A barbell fixed on guided rails. Lets you train squat and press patterns safely with the bar path controlled, ideal for learning and for higher-rep leg work.
startingPosition: For squats: set the bar at shoulder height on the rails, step under it, position it on your upper back, unrack with a wrist turn, and place your feet slightly forward.
steps: Set the safety stops at a height just below your bottom position.
Stand with feet slightly forward of the bar line.
Descend until the thighs are parallel or lower.
Keep the torso upright — the guided bar allows a more vertical position.
Drive up through the whole foot and re-rack by rotating the hooks.
breathing: Inhale and brace on the way down, exhale on the way up.

beginner.note: A great place to learn the squat pattern with less balance demand.

intermediate.note: Combine with free-weight squats for the best of both worlds.

advanced.note: Use for high-rep leg finishers when fatigued.

commonMistakes: Placing the feet directly under the bar (stresses the knees)
safetyTips: Always set the safety stops before you unrack.
Rotate the hooks fully and listen for the click when re-racking.
tip: Step slightly forward of the bar so the knees track naturally over the toes.

name: Calf Raise
description: An isolation movement for the calves using a standing calf raise machine or the leg press. Builds lower-leg strength and ankle stability.
startingPosition: Place the balls of your feet on the platform edge with heels hanging free. Position your shoulders under the pads (standing version) and stand tall.
steps: Keep the knees straight but not locked.
Lower the heels slowly until you feel a deep stretch in the calves.
Pause for one second at the bottom.
Rise as high as possible onto the balls of the feet.
Hold the top squeeze for one second, then lower slowly.
breathing: Inhale as you lower, exhale as you rise.

beginner.note: Bodyweight or light load, full range of motion.

intermediate.note: Add a 2-second pause at the bottom to remove the stretch reflex.

advanced.note: Train calves 2–3 times per week — they recover quickly.

commonMistakes: Partial reps at the top only
safetyTips: Use a full stretch but never a painful one.
Hold the machine handles for balance during heavy sets.
whenToStop: Cramping that does not ease when you stop
alternatives: Single-Leg Calf Raise on a step
tip: The bottom stretch is where calves grow — slow it down and pause.

name: Shoulder Press
description: A guided overhead press that builds shoulder strength on a fixed path. Safer for beginners than free-weight pressing overhead.
startingPosition: Adjust the seat so the handles are level with your ears. Sit back against the pad and grip the handles with palms forward.
steps: Set the seat height so the handles start at ear level.
Press the handles overhead until the arms are extended but not locked hard.
Keep your lower back against the pad — no arching.
Lower slowly until the elbows are just below shoulder height.
Keep the wrists stacked over the elbows throughout.
breathing: Exhale as you press up, inhale as you lower.

beginner.note: Start light; the shoulders respond best to controlled reps.

intermediate.note: Slow the negative to 3 seconds.

advanced.note: Pair with lateral raises for complete shoulder development.

commonMistakes: Arching the lower back to press more
Lowering the handles too far (past the ears)
safetyTips: Keep the back flat on the pad — if it leaves the pad, reduce the weight.
Stop immediately on any sharp pinching pain in the shoulder.
tip: Imagine pushing the machine away from you, not just the handles up.

name: Lateral Raise Machine
description: A guided side-raise movement that isolates the middle deltoid — the muscle that creates shoulder width.
startingPosition: Sit with your upper arms against the pads, elbows bent at about 90°, torso tall against the backrest.
steps: Adjust the seat so the machine pivot aligns with your shoulder joint.
Raise your upper arms out to the sides until they are level with your shoulders.
Lead with the elbows, not the hands.
Pause briefly at shoulder height.
Lower slowly, resisting the weight all the way down.
breathing: Exhale as you raise, inhale as you lower.

beginner.note: Light weight, perfect form — the lateral head is small but proud.

intermediate.note: Add a 1-second hold at the top.

advanced.note: Drop sets work brilliantly here — but keep every rep clean.

commonMistakes: Gripping too hard and leading with the hands
safetyTips: Stop at shoulder height — higher turns it into a trap shrug and stresses the joint.
Keep the neck relaxed.
whenToStop: Pinching pain at the top of the range
tip: Imagine pouring water from a jug at the top — pinky slightly up, elbow leading.

name: Cable Lateral Raise
description: A cable version of the lateral raise that keeps tension on the muscle through the whole range — even at the bottom where dumbbells go light.
startingPosition: Set the pulley at the lowest position. Stand side-on to the stack, holding the handle in the far hand with the cable crossing in front of your legs.
steps: Stand tall with a soft bend in the elbow.
Raise the arm out to the side to shoulder height in a smooth arc.
Keep the wrist neutral — the cable does the work, not the hand.
Pause for a beat at the top.
Lower slowly; the cable stays loaded even at the bottom.
breathing: Exhale as you raise, inhale as you lower.

beginner.note: Stand far enough from the stack that the cable is never slack.

intermediate.note: Slightly lean away from the stack for a longer lever arm.

advanced.note: Try the "behind the back" setup for a stronger stretch.

commonMistakes: Letting the cable go slack at the bottom
Bending the elbow during the rep
safetyTips: Keep the shoulder down and away from the ear throughout.
Choose a weight that allows a full stop at the top.
tip: The bottom half of the rep matters here — control the cable, never let it yank you.

name: Biceps Curl Machine
description: A guided curl that isolates the biceps on a fixed path. Perfect for learning the curl pattern and for high-quality finishing sets.
startingPosition: Sit with your chest against the pad and upper arms resting fully on the support. Grip the handles with palms facing up.
steps: Adjust the seat so your elbows align with the machine pivot.
Curl the handles up until the biceps are fully contracted.
Squeeze hard for one second at the top.
Lower slowly until the arms are nearly straight.
Keep the upper arms glued to the pad at all times.
breathing: Exhale as you curl up, inhale as you lower.

beginner.note: The machine teaches the curl groove before free weights.

intermediate.note: Slow negatives (3 seconds) transform this exercise.

advanced.note: Use as the final biceps exercise on arm day.

commonMistakes: Lifting the elbows off the pad
Dropping the weight on the way down
safetyTips: Keep the wrists straight — curling the wrists shifts stress to the forearms.
Reduce the weight if you cannot lower it slowly.
tip: On the way down, imagine unrolling the arm slowly — the negative builds biceps strength.

name: Cable Curl
description: A cable curl with constant tension from bottom to top. The cable keeps the biceps working even at the top where dumbbells rest.
startingPosition: Attach a straight or EZ bar to the low pulley. Stand tall with elbows pinned to your sides and the bar resting at your thighs.
steps: Stand close enough that the cable is taut at the bottom.
Curl the bar to your shoulders without moving the elbows.
Squeeze the biceps at the top for one second.
Lower slowly, fighting the cable all the way down.
Keep the torso upright — no leaning back.
breathing: Exhale as you curl, inhale as you lower.

beginner.note: The constant tension teaches you to feel the biceps working.

intermediate.note: Step back slightly for tension through the full range.

advanced.note: Finish with a 10-second isometric hold at 90°.

commonMistakes: Leaning back to move the weight
safetyTips: Elbows stay pinned — if they move, the shoulders take over.
Control the return; never let the weight stack drop.
tip: Imagine curling the bar toward your face while your elbows stay nailed to your ribs.

name: Triceps Pushdown
description: The classic cable pushdown for the triceps — the muscle that makes up two-thirds of upper-arm size. Simple, safe, and highly effective.
startingPosition: Attach a rope or bar to the high pulley. Stand facing the stack with elbows pinned to your sides, forearms parallel to the floor.
steps: Grip the rope or bar with the elbows glued to your ribs.
Push down until the arms are fully extended.
Split the rope ends apart at the bottom if using a rope.
Squeeze the triceps for one second.
Let the forearms rise until the elbows are at about 90° — no higher.
breathing: Exhale as you push down, inhale on the return.

beginner.note: Light weight, strict form, full lockout on every rep.

intermediate.note: Add a pause at the bottom of each rep.

advanced.note: Use as a finisher with a controlled 3-second negative.

commonMistakes: Elbows flaring out from the body
Leaning over the cable to push more
safetyTips: Stand tall; if you must lean, the weight is too heavy.
Keep the wrists straight throughout.
tip: Lock out fully and squeeze — the last inch of the pushdown is the most valuable part.

name: Triceps Extension
description: An overhead cable extension that stretches the triceps long head — the part of the triceps most visible from the side. Great for complete arm development.
startingPosition: Attach a rope to the low pulley. Face away, hold the rope behind your head, and hinge slightly forward with elbows pointing up.
steps: Keep the elbows high and pointing forward, close to your ears.
Extend the arms until they are straight overhead.
Squeeze the triceps at full lockout.
Return slowly until the forearms fold back down — feel the stretch.
Keep the upper arms completely still throughout.
breathing: Exhale as you extend, inhale as you return.

beginner.note: Start with a light load; the overhead position feels unusual at first.

intermediate.note: Pause for a second in the stretched position.

advanced.note: Use a slow 3-second stretch on the way down.

commonMistakes: Elbows drifting out to the sides
Turning it into a lat pulldown
safetyTips: Brace the core to protect the lower back in the hinged position.
Stop if you feel shoulder discomfort overhead.
whenToStop: Shoulder pain in the overhead position
tip: The stretch at the bottom is the goal — take your time getting there.

name: Treadmill
description: The most popular cardio machine in the gym. Walking, jogging, or running — the treadmill scales to any fitness level and builds endurance.
startingPosition: Stand on the side rails, start the belt at a slow speed, and step on once it is moving. Keep your body upright and eyes forward.
steps: Always start at a slow speed and step on carefully.
Walk or jog with a tall posture — no leaning on the handrails.
Gradually increase speed or incline to your target intensity.
Use the "talk test": you should be able to speak short sentences.
Cool down with 2–3 minutes of easy walking before stepping off.
breathing: Breathe rhythmically — in through the nose, out through the mouth. If you cannot talk, slow down.

beginner.note: Aim for a pace where conversation is possible. Add incline for intensity without speed.

intermediate.note: Try 1 minute faster / 1 minute easier repeats.

advanced.note: Mix incline walking and tempo runs across the week.

commonMistakes: Stepping off while the belt is still moving
safetyTips: Use the emergency stop clip.
Never step onto a moving belt at speed.
Stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness, or unusual breathlessness.
whenToStop: Pain in the knees that worsens with each step
tip: A 1–2% incline mimics outdoor walking and is easier on the knees.

name: Cross Trainer
description: Also called an elliptical. A low-impact, full-body cardio machine that protects the joints while raising the heart rate.
startingPosition: Step on the largest pedal first, grip the handles, and begin pedalling smoothly. Keep your torso tall.
steps: Start pedalling to wake the console, then choose your programme.
Keep a tall posture with a light grip on the handles.
Push and pull the handles to involve the upper body.
Maintain a smooth, gliding rhythm — no bouncing.
Gradually increase resistance rather than only speed.
breathing: Steady, rhythmic breathing. You should be able to hold a conversation.

beginner.note: Focus on a smooth stroke before adding resistance.

intermediate.note: Alternate 2 minutes easy / 2 minutes hard.

advanced.note: Use the programmes or manual intervals for variety.

commonMistakes: Going too fast with no resistance
safetyTips: Use the step platforms when getting on and off.
Keep knees tracking in line with the toes.
tip: Increase resistance before speed — that is where the fitness benefit lives.

name: Exercise Bike
description: A seated, joint-friendly way to build lower-body endurance and cardiovascular fitness. Great for beginners and for active recovery days.
startingPosition: Adjust the seat so your knee has a slight bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke. Sit tall with a light grip on the bars.
steps: Adjust the seat height first — a slight knee bend at the bottom.
Pedal at a comfortable cadence for a 3-minute warm-up.
Build to your target resistance and pace.
Keep the hips still — no rocking side to side.
Cool down with 2–3 minutes of easy spinning.
breathing: Steady breathing; the "talk test" is your intensity guide.

beginner.note: Comfortable resistance, steady cadence around 60–70 rpm.

intermediate.note: Raise resistance for 2 minutes, recover for 2, repeat.

advanced.note: Combine seated and standing climbs for intensity.

commonMistakes: Seat set too low or too high
safetyTips: Check the pedals are secure before riding.
Stop if you feel knee pain during the stroke.
tip: Your hips should stay perfectly still — if they rock, the seat is too high.

name: Rowing Machine
description: A full-body cardio machine that works the legs, back, and arms in one smooth stroke. Excellent for posture and total-body conditioning.
startingPosition: Sit on the seat, strap your feet in, and grip the handle. Start with knees bent, shins vertical, arms extended, and torso leaning slightly forward.
steps: The stroke order is: legs → body → arms.
Drive with the legs first while the arms stay straight.
Lean back slightly as the legs finish, then pull the handle to your ribs.
Return in reverse: arms out, body over, knees bend.
Keep the chain level and the movement smooth — no jerking.
breathing: Exhale on the drive, inhale on the recovery. The recovery should be roughly twice as long as the drive.

beginner.note: Learn the stroke order before chasing speed.

intermediate.note: Aim for 22–26 strokes per minute for endurance.

advanced.note: Add 250 m sprints with 1-minute rests.

commonMistakes: Pulling with the arms too early
Sliding the seat before the legs finish
Rowing with a very fast, sloppy rhythm
safetyTips: Keep the back straight — the power comes from the legs.
Stop if your lower back tightens painfully.
tip: Think "legs, body, arms — arms, body, legs". The order is everything.

name: Stair Climber
description: A continuously revolving staircase that delivers a serious lower-body burn and a big cardiovascular challenge in a short time.
startingPosition: Step on at the lowest speed, grip the rails lightly, and stand tall with your whole foot landing on each step.
steps: Start at a slow speed to find your rhythm.
Stand tall — do not lean your weight on the handrails.
Place the whole foot on each step, not just the toes.
Gradually increase speed to your target level.
Cool down for 2–3 minutes at a slow pace before stepping off.
breathing: Deep, steady breaths. This machine is intense — slow the speed if you are gasping.

beginner.note: Hold the rails lightly for balance only.

intermediate.note: Keep hands off the rails as much as possible.

advanced.note: Alternate 2 minutes hard / 2 minutes recovery.

commonMistakes: Leaning the whole upper body on the rails
safetyTips: Hold the rails if you feel unsteady — safety first.
Step off only when the machine is at the slowest speed.
tip: Hands barely touching the rails doubles the work of the glutes and core.

name: Dumbbells
targetMuscles: Every muscle group (used in dozens of exercises)
description: The most versatile equipment in the gym. Dumbbells train each side independently, fix imbalances, and offer endless exercise variety for every muscle.
startingPosition: Choose a weight you can control for the full set. For any dumbbell exercise, keep the wrists neutral and the core braced.
steps: Pick a weight you can lift with perfect form for every rep.
Set your body position for the exercise first, then lift.
Move through a full range of motion.
Keep both sides moving evenly — dumbbells expose imbalances.
Return the dumbbells to the rack, never drop them on the floor.
breathing: Exhale on the effort, inhale on the return — for every exercise.

beginner.note: Master the basic moves: press, row, curl, squat, lunge.

intermediate.note: Progress weight in small jumps — 2 kg is a real jump for small muscles.

advanced.note: Use unilateral work (one side at a time) to fix weaknesses.

commonMistakes: Choosing weights that are too heavy to control
Uneven range of motion side to side
safetyTips: Never drop dumbbells — lower them safely to the floor or rack.
Start light on any new exercise until the technique is solid.
tip: If you cannot lower a weight slowly, it is too heavy — control is the secret to results.

name: Barbells
description: The heart of strength training. Barbells allow the heaviest loads and the biggest compound movements: squats, deadlifts, presses, and rows.
startingPosition: Learn each lift with an empty bar first. Always train inside a rack with safeties for squats and presses.
steps: Learn each barbell lift with an empty bar or PVC pipe first.
Set up the rack, safeties, and collars before loading plates.
Load plates evenly on both sides and secure the collars.
Brace hard before every rep of every set.
Re-rack carefully and strip the bar when finished.
breathing: Brace with a big breath before each rep; exhale after the sticking point.

beginner.note: Learn proper technique from a qualified trainer before performing barbell lifts independently.

intermediate.note: Progress by adding small, consistent weight jumps.

advanced.note: Periodise your training and schedule regular deload weeks.

safetyTips: Learn proper technique from a qualified trainer before performing these exercises independently.
Always use collars and safeties. Never attempt unsafe maximum-weight lifts.
Train with a spotter on heavy sets.
whenToStop: Any sharp pain during a lift
Inability to maintain a neutral spine
tip: The empty bar is not embarrassing — it is the smartest tool you own for learning movement.

name: Kettlebells
description: Cannonball-shaped weights with a handle, built for flowing, full-body movements like swings, goblet squats, and carries. Strength and conditioning in one tool.
startingPosition: Start with light kettlebells. For most lifts, set the feet shoulder-width, brace the core, and keep the back neutral.
steps: Choose a light bell and learn the movement pattern without load first.
Keep the back neutral — the hips do the hinging, not the spine.
Move smoothly; kettlebell work is about flow, not jerking.
Set the bell down carefully between sets, never drop it.
Progress in skill (harder movements) before progressing in weight.
breathing: Exhale forcefully on the effort (the top of a swing, the press lockout), inhale on the way down.

beginner.note: Master the goblet squat and deadlift pattern first.

intermediate.note: Learn the two-hand swing with light weight before anything else.

advanced.note: Progress to cleans, snatches, and Turkish get-ups only with coaching.

commonMistakes: Squatting the swing instead of hinging
Using the arms to lift instead of the hips
Dropping the bell on the floor
safetyTips: Learn kettlebell technique from a qualified trainer — especially ballistic moves like the swing.
Give yourself space: check the area around you before swinging.
tip: The swing is a hip hinge, not a squat — the bell floats, the hips snap.

name: Weight Plates
targetMuscles: Every muscle group (loaded carries, plate exercises)
description: Weight plates are not just for loading barbells — they are training tools themselves for carries, twists, presses, and core work.
startingPosition: Grip the plate firmly at the edges or through the centre hole, depending on the exercise.
steps: Choose a plate size you can handle comfortably.
Keep the plate close to the body when carrying or pressing.
Move slowly and deliberately — plate work rewards control.
Return plates to the storage tree when done.
breathing: Exhale on effort, inhale on the return.

beginner.note: Try plate goblet squats, plate rows, and short carries.

intermediate.note: Add overhead plate carries for core and shoulder stability.

advanced.note: Combine carries with squats or lunges for conditioning.

commonMistakes: Letting the plate pull the shoulders forward on carries
Using a plate that is too heavy to press overhead safely
safetyTips: Always re-rack plates on the storage tree.
Press plates overhead only with a weight you can control.
tip: A plate carry is one of the best core exercises nobody does — walk tall and breathe.

name: Ab Crunch Machine
description: A guided crunch machine that trains the abs with resistance on a fixed path. Easy on the neck and lower back when set up correctly.
startingPosition: Sit with your chest against the pad (or grip the handles overhead, depending on the design). Adjust the seat so the pivot aligns with your waist.
steps: Adjust the seat so the machine pivot sits at your waistline.
Curl your torso forward by contracting the abs.
Exhale fully as you crunch.
Pause for a second in the contracted position.
Return slowly without letting the weight stack drop.
breathing: Exhale hard as you crunch, inhale as you return.

beginner.note: Light resistance — feel the abs working, not the hips.

intermediate.note: Add a pause at the contraction point.

advanced.note: Use as a finisher after compound core work.

commonMistakes: Pulling with the arms or hips instead of the abs
Rounding the lower back under load
safetyTips: Keep the movement in the abs — if the hips or arms are doing the work, reduce the weight.
Avoid if you have a history of lower-back problems without professional advice.
tip: Exhale everything out at the top — the abs contract hardest when the lungs are empty.

name: Cable Crunch
description: A kneeling crunch against cable resistance. The cable lets you load the abs progressively, unlike bodyweight crunches.
startingPosition: Attach a rope to the high pulley. Kneel facing the stack, hold the rope beside your head, and let the cable stretch you slightly upright.
steps: Kneel about a metre from the stack with the rope by your ears.
Keep the hips fixed — the crunch happens only in the spine.
Curl the ribs toward the pelvis, exhaling fully.
Squeeze the abs hard at the bottom.
Return slowly until you feel a stretch in the abs.
breathing: Exhale completely as you crunch down, inhale on the way up.

beginner.note: Light weight; the movement is smaller than it looks.

intermediate.note: Pause for 2 seconds at the bottom of each rep.

advanced.note: Increase the load gradually — the abs respond to progressive overload too.

commonMistakes: Hinging at the hips instead of curling the spine
Pulling the rope with the arms
Letting the cable yank the body up
safetyTips: Keep the arms passive — they only hold the rope in place.
Kneel on a mat to protect the knees.
tip: The abs only move the ribcage about 30° — the rest is wasted motion and hip work.

name: Back Extension Bench
description: Also called the Roman chair or 45° hyperextension. Strengthens the entire back chain — the muscles that protect your spine in every lift.
startingPosition: Position yourself face down with the hip pad just below your hip bones, feet hooked under the pads, body in a straight line.
steps: Set the pad so your hips can hinge freely.
Start with the body in one straight line from head to heels.
Lower slowly by hinging at the hips until you feel a hamstring stretch.
Rise back up by squeezing the glutes — not by arching the lower back.
Stop at the straight-line position; never hyperextend backwards.
breathing: Inhale on the way down, exhale as you rise.

beginner.note: Bodyweight only; learn the hinge before holding any weight.

intermediate.note: Hold a light plate to the chest once the movement is perfect.

advanced.note: Progress weight slowly — quality of hinge matters more than load.

commonMistakes: Hyperextending the back at the top
Rounding the back at the bottom
Setting the pad too high or too low
safetyTips: Never swing or bounce — every rep should be slow and controlled.
If you have a history of back issues, check with a professional before using this bench.
tip: Think "push the hips into the pad" as you rise — that cue fires the glutes.
